pitch_detail.notes: An easy ramp rising to the right ends at the first station.
Face climbing past three bolts reaches a crack that becomes a chimney; a ledge tops it.
Sustained and the hardest pitch. A 12 m leftward traverse from the belay passes a bolt and gets you into a finger-to-hand crack, which is followed with jams and layaways.
The crack goes on, over a small lip, to ledges and a station above.
Step right from the belay onto discontinuous cracks up to a small roof, step left to a piton, then continue up and left to a bolt that gets you into a prominent crack system just under a ledge.

Follow the crack system from the ledge to a series of small roofs. When gear thins out, a piton is used to get past the crux to a station above. Three bolts above this station are there for anyone completing the line.

review.changed: Wrote 6 pitches; a seventh was attempted but not completed. No rappel table (stations are mentioned only in general terms).

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the face using left-facing flakes and cracks, then discontinuous, partly hollow flakes to a right-facing flake and crack that reaches the right end of a big ledge. Walk left along the ledge, watching for loose rock, and belay off a slung block.

Shift a few metres up and right to an evident vertical flake-corner system and follow it about 30 m. Then step out of the corner to the right for a few metres and continue on holds, flakes and finger or hand cracks, staying parallel to the corner on its left so as to dodge the roofs inside it.

Get back into the corner system and carry on to an orange roof, which you pass on the left. Above is a smaller left-facing corner (a big loose dagger sits in it, so stay clear), then a second roof offering solid hand jams and big holds. Over it, step right into a deep alcove beneath a large chockstone to belay.

Wriggle up the narrow hole behind the chockstone, or layback up its outer face with good gear (5.10a). Above it go left into a sustained shallow left-facing corner, ending at a cramped stance under the last headwall.

Aim for a shallow corner shaped like a crescent, passing a fixed piton and a bolt. A hard step leftward across thin face is the crux. A sustained left-facing corner with good gear comes next; around 25 m up, ease rightward onto gentler ground and a roomy ledge below another left-facing corner.

Stem and jam the pleasant left-facing corner for about 10 m, then follow easier terrain for a full rope length with many belay choices, watching for loose rock. This joins the upper South Ridge, which is scrambled to the summit.
About 30 m of awkward ice leads to a long snow ramp ending in an ice cave behind pillars.
Leave the cave and climb 20 m of steep ice. It was originally given WI4 but was harder, WI5-, when climbed. Snow follows to a tree anchor.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches. Descent is a rappel of the route; no station list so no rappel table. Approach (a long ski or sled in the Blaeberry) not included.

pitch_detail.notes: A rambling opening leads to mostly unbroken cracks of hand and fist size. Climb directly up and belay either inside the cracks or on a stance next to a pale tree. Then reset the belay roughly 3 m lower and to the right, at the foot of the thin curving splitter. Protection is limited on the moderate ground, so expect some runouts.
Follow the attractive right-curving crack, mostly mid-size cams (grey, purple, green). At its top, rock left and traverse back into the main corner system to belay.

From the belay go up and left over a small roof, which takes you out of the main corner system and onto a hand crack on the face. About 35 m of varied cracks follow, ending at a stance at the top of a finger crack.

Take the blocky corner, being careful of loose rocks on the ledges midway. At the top of the blocky part step right using good face holds to reach the foot of the enormous right-facing corner that forms the Daylight Pillar. Belay on a small stance.

This is the Daylight Pillar itself. A sequence of finger cracks, hand cracks and an off-width ends in a brief squeeze to the pillar top. Helpful cheater holds keep the grade friendly even to people wary of wide cracks. From the top, scramble left to the west ridge to descend or finish at the false summit.

Climb a right-facing corner to a small ledge about 5 m up, then continue up the corner's left side. The hard section is short, thin and technical, with four fixed pins; a 2-3 m stretch is 5.10+/11-. Past it, step back right onto a small ledge and a good hand crack. The rest is mostly 5.10. Belay on a ledge beside a bush.
Easy ground up and right from the belay to a ledge by a bush beneath the big roof.

Leave the belay to the right and take the steep hand crack in the corner, over the roof and into the big left-facing corner. Climb it to its end, then a strenuous move out to the right gets through a second roof. Hold a #1 or #2 cam back for the roof. A fantastic pitch.
A very short pitch: step left and face climb past three bolts to a small ledge. Linking it with pitch 3 may be best.
Go straight up from the belay on the cracks to the right. Where the crack steepens, face climb right past two bolts and switch into the next crack right, which leads to a good ledge.
Step right off the ledge and work up and rightward over easier ground, joining the fifth pitch of Common Knowledge.

Scramble to the saddle between the South Pillar and the false summit of Rexford. From there you can scramble to the top of the pillar, or drop west through the notch to the regular west ridge route, or continue up the south ridge for 2-4 more pitches of low fifth class up to 5.8.

review.changed: Wrote 7 pitches (the text lists a final fourth-class pitch beyond the stored 6). Lengths are marked approximate in the text.
review.other_findings: Stored pitches 6; text lists 6 roped pitches plus a fourth-class scramble.

pitch_detail.notes: The line starts on a finger crack to the right of a mossy groove. Place a sling on the tree beneath the loose block, then go left and upward past a dead tree into an alcove.
A short crack on the right goes over a small bulge. Then cross a block to the left and enter the trees to reach a spacious ledge.
A right-leaning crack goes up to a piton clipped before the mantle, and a few more moves reach a large ledge.
Face climbing left of the corner gets you to a good stance. Step right into a groove that you stem up, ending in the trees.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches. Descent is a third-class scramble to the gully on climber's left, already stored implicitly.

pitch_detail.notes: Go up the left corner to a bushy ledge, then a flake, finishing left of a roof by pulling on trees to the top of First Ledge. The pitch can be avoided by a low fifth-class gully to the right.
Take the face to the left of the prominent corner, scrambling up cracks and shelves to Crescent Ledge. Tree belay.

Reset the belay at the far left end of Crescent Ledge, crossing a big boulder on the way. Scramble up a corner whose right wall has horizontal cracks, reaching a small ledge; then blocky twin cracks go up and left. From the next ledge scramble leftward to a tree resembling an octopus, which serves as the belay.
Low-angle blocks and ledges lead to the top. Rappel from trees to descend.

A short M3 boulder problem guards the start of the gully proper. Beyond it wade steep snow, then a slightly longer M4- boulder problem. Belay from the small tree on the right side, with a piton available to back it up.

Go up the steep snow ramp. When cold this may be easy snice, but with a thin cover it climbs as chossy mixed ground. Snow and turf continue to a piton belay on the left. Above, the gully broadens and you pick your own way to the sub-summit, with some optional M3 boulder problems.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches; the text describes only these before the gully opens up.

pitch_detail.notes: Take the corner that trends left and continue into the first crack system, which ends on a large ledge holding two stacked boulders.

Direct variation. Move the belay up onto the prominent boulder, then pass three bolts on surprisingly sporty moves. Easy slab leads up left, followed by a rightward move past a bolt into a tricky groove. The second bolt there marks the crux; two more bolts lie straight above, ending at a ledge. Keep a 0.2 cam for the stretch after the second bolt, which feels bold. Belay on one bolt plus thin gear.
Traverse left to the arete and climb it with good protection. Belay on or just short of the massive ledge; the top can be reached by scrambling from there.

rappel_detail.notes: Lands on a big sideways-growing tree on the west face.
Continue to a tat anchor on climber's right.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches and a 3-station rappel table from the listed descent.

pitch_detail.notes: A steep but short ice step, protected in the rock to its right, is followed by runout snow and mixed ground up into the cleft. Below the crux a small solid crack makes a good rock belay. The initial belay is poor but can be backed up with rock gear about 6 ft up and right.

The crux. Difficulties start at once with steep, thin, hollow ice over a featureless slab; rock gear on the right side of the cleft allows stemming and rests. Above the ice crux the angle eases to rambling snow and ice toward a possible cornice finish. Over the top, cracks in a small overhanging roof give belay options.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches; none graded separately in the text.

pitch_detail.notes: Easy climbing on three bolts.
About seven bolts.
Ten bolts. At the end of the pitch veer right at the ledge to the anchors there; going left finishes on Time Machine instead.
Two bolts plus gear to 3 inches.
One bolt plus gear to 3 inches.
Starts at 5.8 and eases to 5.5 for the finish.

review.changed: Wrote 6 pitches. Most pitches are around 30 m or less. No rappel table: anchors are all bolted but individual stations are not listed.

pitch_detail.notes: A steep 20 m pillar with a thin exit to the anchor. Then walk about 100 m up a snow slope to a wide shield of ice.
Lower-angle ice to mushrooms that end on an ice ledge under hanging daggers.

pitch_detail.anchor: 2 bolt anchor on a tiny ledge
pitch_detail.notes: Right and up from the belay along 12 bolts of steep, pumpy drytooling, getting over an overhang for the last three bolts.

Work up and to the right into a steep corner system where placements feel insecure; six bolts protect it, and a couple more higher up may help depending on how the ice has formed. Step left onto the hanging ice and work out how to reach its front face. About 20 m of dead vertical ice on the dagger follows, then trend right where it lies back to an ice belay.
Three steps of steep ice with rests between lead to a two-bolt anchor that may be hard to spot; otherwise belay in the sheltered cave behind the last 5 m of ice.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches. No rappel table: the rappel description mixes rope lengths and a snow walk and is not a clean station list.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep climbing that may offer chandelier ice and bulges. Belay on a shelf about halfway up, right or left depending on the side climbed.
Pure power ice climbing, steep all the way.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches; route is about 100 m, relentlessly steep. No per-pitch grades are given, so none are written.

pitch_detail.notes: Follow the cracked prow, with an easy roof about three quarters up, to a decent ledge. Gear belay with a fixed nut.
The prow and its cracks continue up to a narrow notch at the finish. Gear belay backed by a fixed nut.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches. No rappel table (descent options are described but not as a station list).

pitch_detail.notes: Easy arete climbing at a gentle angle ends at a belay on one bolt.

Head for the roof with its cracks. Clip a bolt and go directly to the roof cracks, or angle right to the corner for better gear. From the foot of the gentle corner, move left onto a wide crack and climb it until it ends at a one-bolt belay.

Climb the deep corner up to a steeper one containing a finger crack. At its top go left to clip a bolt and climb the crack. When the crack veers left, cross the slab past a bolt to the final belay. The last anchor has two bolts, but the right-hand one was not fully tightened, so do not trust it.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches; no grades per pitch in the text, so none given.

pitch_detail.notes: Begin in a brief, very thin corner on stemming and face holds. Use the crack above plus some blocky ground to its right until you commit fully to the thin-hands splitter. A brief wider stretch accepts #1 cams deep in the crack, so carry two. A small tree gives a belay or a rappel point. This pitch works well as a stand-alone single pitch.

A mossy, mediocre-rock pitch: from the tree go up and left on a gently right-leaning crack past poor rock into a long stemming corner. The fun 5.9 stemming has a damp mossy crack for protection (mostly #3 size) and ends at a very good belay ledge. Easier terrain above leads out, but the route has been climbed no higher.

From the base of the cliff go through easy terrain and angle left to the large square block seen halfway up. Dirt and loose rock are likely; a couple of tricky moves in the last corner gain the ledge on top of the block.
The thin crack goes straight up then slightly left, with a final traverse back right to a ledge. Face holds appear where the crack thins out.
A brief but excellent hand crack finishes the wall. Belay on gear just past the top, or from trees back from the edge. It can easily be linked with the pitch below.
Trend left until you are under the belay stance, then go straight up.
Climb the corner with twin cracks to beneath a small roof, then go straight up the finger crack until you can balance left onto easier ground to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 2 pitches; descent by the standard rappel route (no station list).

pitch_detail.notes: Begin in a right-facing corner that offers several cracks. Work slightly left, passing a ledge and getting behind a big flake, to a modest stance at the base of a finger crack on the face.
Go straight up the face using fingerlocks until a small roof forces a move left, then to the base of the summit headwall.
Enjoyable climbing with a few tricky sections leads straight to the summit.
